content: The document outlines detailed strategies and procedures for the surveillance, prevention, and elimination of rabies, particularly focusing on cases transmitted by dogs. It emphasizes the importance of routine epidemiological investigations into suspected or probable rabies cases in dogs. This includes rapid collection and transportation of samples to laboratories for diagnosis, the sampling strategies employed, and methods for monitoring dog vaccination coverage. To verify progress, evidence must demonstrate that enhanced dog rabies surveillance has been in place for at least 24 months after the last detected rabies case.g., wildlife variant, bat lyssavirus, or non-indigenous infection). Post-validation and post-verification plans for rabies surveillance are critical. Contingency plans must also be in place to respond effectively to any reintroduction of rabies, including regulations on animal movement, regular risk assessments of incursions from other regions, and outbreak response strategies. The document also highlights the need for sustainable resource mobilization strategies, including human and financial resources, to support rabies control programs. A bibliography of data sources, including ministry of health records, veterinary service records, and scientific publications, is required, along with a list of abbreviations used in the dossier. The World Health Organization (WHO) has been instrumental in providing technical guidance and support for rabies elimination efforts. Since the launch of the global framework to eliminate human rabies transmitted by dogs by 2030, WHO has collaborated with various organizations, including the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), and the Global Alliance for Rabies Control, to develop a global strategic plan. This plan adopts a country-centric approach to empower national entities to control and eliminate rabies. The report provides updated evidence-based guidance on rabies prevention, control, and elimination. Key updates include surveillance strategies, cross-sectoral system integration, diagnostic improvements, recommendations for human and animal immunization, palliative care in low-resource settings, risk assessment for bite victim management, and processes for validating and verifying zero human deaths from rabies. The recommendations align with WHO’s objectives of improving access to affordable rabies biologics, particularly for underserved populations, and enhancing programmatic feasibility in line with universal health coverage goals. Rabies is a vaccine-preventable disease, and investing in its control and elimination strengthens health systems, improves equity and access to healthcare, and contributes to sustainable development. The collaborative mechanisms required to prevent rabies serve as a model for One Health collaboration at all levels. Eliminating rabies not only addresses this fatal but preventable disease but also builds capacity in the world’s most neglected regions, reducing the burden of pain and suffering, particularly among children.
